thesis.label: Contact-tiered brand and agency email vs creator subscriber platform
thesis.rationale: Campaign Monitor documents design-led email with contact-tiered Lite, Essentials and Premier plans plus agency multi-account features; Kit documents a creator-first platform with a free Newsletter tier and subscriber-tiered Creator and Pro plans for monetisation.

pricing.complexityNote: One or both sides publish four or more rungs — compare the tier you would actually buy, not the entry rung
notes: Campaign Monitor plans: Lite, Essentials, Premier, Enterprise (1 quote-based)

Campaign Monitor: Verified 2026-08-17 from campaignmonitor.com/pricing. Plans: Free trial / Lite / Essentials / Premier / Enterprise. Contact bands on page: 0–500, 501–2,500, …, 50,001+. For 0–500 contacts, official page shows ~10% annual discount figures consistent with monthly floors Lite $13, Essentials $31 (explicit 'then $31/month' copy), Premier $171; annual effective ≈ $11.70 / $27.90 / $153.90. Lite: capped sends (~5× / 2,500 at 500 contacts). Essentials/Premier: unlimited sends. Website Builder add-on $10/mo on lower tiers. Enterprise: contact sales (GDPR/SOC2, custom DPA, invoice/PO). 30-day free trial documented (500 contacts / 500 emails on trial comparison). No forever-free plan on pricing page.

Kit: Verified 2026-08-17 from kit.com/pricing. Newsletter Free $0 with limited automations. Creator from $33/mo ($390/yr) and Pro from $66/mo ($790/yr) at 1,000 subscribers. 14-day free trial; free migrations marketed. Confirm live subscriber slider.

evidence.disclaimer: Neither product has a completed hands-on product test on SoftwareGlimpse — this comparison is research/data-based only.

patch.summary:
Both send newsletters beautifully; they are built for different businesses. Campaign Monitor is for brands and agencies that care about template control, client accounts and on-brand output. Kit is for creators who monetise an audience — paid newsletters, digital products, and automations built around subscriber growth. The billing units reflect that: contact bands on one side, subscriber counts on the other. Buy the one whose unit matches how your list actually grows.

Neither product has a completed hands-on product test on SoftwareGlimpse — this comparison is research/data-based only.
patch.verdict: Campaign Monitor is the better platform when brand consistency and client work are the requirement: drag-and-drop design, template governance, and multi-account handling for agencies running several senders. Kit is the better platform when the list is the business — the free Newsletter tier lets you start at zero, and Creator and Pro add the visual automations, landing pages and product selling that monetisation needs. Cost behaviour differs sharply: Campaign Monitor has no forever-free plan and is trial-only, its Lite plan caps monthly sends so frequent senders upgrade on cadence rather than list size, the Premier jump is large at the same contact band, and past roughly 50,000 contacts you are usually talking to sales; Kit's paid tiers start from $33 per month for Creator and $66 for Pro at 1,000 subscribers and climb with subscribers. Two documented limits: Kit's free Newsletter plan restricts automations, and its ecommerce catalogue depth trails Klaviyo and Omnisend. Poor fit for Campaign Monitor: a solo creator who needs a free start. Poor fit for Kit: an agency needing client account separation and strict template control.
patch.pricingNotes: Campaign Monitor has no forever-free plan — trial only — with Lite, Essentials and Premier priced by contact band from $13 per month and a custom Enterprise tier; Lite carries monthly send caps, the Essentials-to-Premier step is steep at the same contact band, and 50,001+ contacts typically requires sales. Kit is freemium: a free Newsletter plan with limited automations, then Creator from $33 per month and Pro from $66 per month at 1,000 subscribers on monthly billing, with annual discounts published and pricing rising as subscribers grow. Model your own send frequency against contact bands on one side and subscriber count on the other.

scenarios: Agencies managing email for multiple client accounts
Brands needing template control and design consistency
Marketing teams whose list grows faster than send frequency
Creators monetising a newsletter with paid subscriptions or products
Writers who need a free tier to start and grow into automations
Solo operators wanting landing pages and forms in the same tool

scenarioRecommendations.scenario: Agency sending on behalf of eight client brands
scenarioRecommendations.rationale: Multi-account and agency features plus template governance are the documented strength; Kit is built around one creator's audience, not client separation.

scenarioRecommendations.scenario: Creator launching a paid newsletter with no budget yet
scenarioRecommendations.rationale: The free Newsletter tier starts at zero and monetisation tooling is native, whereas Campaign Monitor is trial-only with no forever-free plan.

scenarioRecommendations.scenario: Sending several campaigns a week to a modest list
scenarioRecommendations.rationale: Watch the caps on both sides: Campaign Monitor's Lite send limits push frequent senders up a tier regardless of list size, and Kit's free plan limits the automations that make frequent sending manageable.

outcomes.reason: Campaign Monitor researched starting price from $13/mo; Kit researched starting price from $33/mo; a free plan is researched. Contact-based packaging can change the real TCO. Contact bands against subscriber counts: the billing unit differs, so the cheaper option changes with list shape rather than list size alone.

Email send limits depend on plan rungs for Campaign Monitor and Kit. Confirm current send and automation caps before purchase. Monthly send caps on the entry rung push frequent senders up a tier regardless of list size — the binding constraint is cadence, not contacts.

Kit leads on automation (6/10 vs 7/10) from approved SoftwareGlimpse editorial assessments — not hands-on lab testing. Automations are restricted on the free creator rung and sold up the ladder on both sides, so test the tier you would actually run.

Campaign Monitor leads on templates (9/10 vs 8/10) from approved SoftwareGlimpse editorial assessments — not hands-on lab testing. Template governance across multiple client accounts against creator layouts built around a single voice.

landing pages: Kit shows stronger researched availability (limited vs supported). Landing pages and forms are bundled where monetising an audience is the point, rather than treated as a marketing add-on.

Kit leads on value for money (6/10 vs 8/10) from approved SoftwareGlimpse editorial assessments — not hands-on lab testing. A steep step between mid and premium tiers at the same contact band on one side; steadily subscriber-driven cost growth on the other.
